case20v1-q.stats.basics:
The Average Gold User at Lekhni Pay

A teaching case on descriptive statistics for product managers

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 12 October 2026, Gayatri Vartak sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of Lekhni Pay's Bengaluru office with a single sentence from the finance team on her laptop: "We need one number for the monthly cashback ceiling by Friday." Girish Vaze, the chief financial officer, would take that number to the board on 16 October. The Diwali campaign for Lekhni Gold, the company's paid tier, was due to go live on 26 October, and Diwali itself fell on 8 November. If the ceiling was approved, marketing could print it on every banner. If it was wrong, the company would either strangle a promising launch or pay out cashback it had never planned for.

Gayatri, head of product for Gold, had a spreadsheet open. At the top was a figure everyone in the building had been quoting for a week: the average Gold user spends ₹2,555 a month through the app. She suspected that the figure was true and still the wrong thing to build a promise on. She had until Friday to decide how to turn it into a ceiling.

2. Company background

Lekhni Pay was founded in 2019 by two former bankers who noticed that Indians paid dozens of recurring bills, among them electricity, piped gas, broadband, school fees and housing-society dues, through a patchwork of apps and counters. The company built a bill-payment app on top of UPI, the interoperable payments rail run by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), and registered as a bill payment operator under the Reserve Bank of India's framework. Revenue came from small fees on convenience payments, from commissions paid by billers, and, since 2025, from Lekhni Gold, a subscription tier that bundled reminders, a family dashboard and monthly cashback.

The competitive field was crowded. PhonePe and Paytm had enormous user bases and aggressive merchant networks; CRED had cultivated an affluent audience; Google Pay and Amazon Pay were never far from any user's home screen. Lekhni's edge was depth in the dull categories, and its Gold tier, with 1,20,000 users active in September 2026, was its first serious attempt to charge for it. The company employed about 340 people, with engineers in Bengaluru and Pune and a growth team in Singapore.

3. The situation

Gold's current cashback was a modest fixed ₹10 a month. For Diwali, the growth team wanted to replace it with a percentage: 1 per cent of everything a Gold user pays through the app in a month. Girish's team needed to know what that would cost. The simplest route was the number already in circulation, the average spend. But Gayatri had learned to be careful about averages, and she asked Gauri Venugopal, a data scientist working from Toronto, to pull the September spending of 40 randomly chosen Gold users, so that the team could look at the shape of the data and not only its centre.

Gauri's file arrived at what was evening in Bengaluru and early morning in Toronto. Her covering note was short: "The mean is ₹2,554.50 and the median is ₹965. Please do not budget off either until you have looked at the tail." Exhibit 1 reproduces the 40 values and the statistics computed from them. Thirty-five of the 40 users spent less than the mean. The two statistics were not close, and the reason, visible in the sorted list, was that five users spent ₹3,100 or more, and two of them spent ₹18,500 and ₹31,000. A rent-and-fees payer and a small landlord paying society dues for several flats were probably among them; Gauri had no field to confirm it.

The five-number story in Exhibit 1b is stark. (The quartiles here are Tukey hinges, the median of each half; Excel's or pandas' default interpolation gives 682.5 and 1,505, and the exclusive method gives 667.5 and 1,555, so state the convention whenever you quote a quartile.) A quarter of users spent ₹675 or less and a quarter spent ₹1,530 or more, so the middle half of the base sat in a band less than ₹900 wide. Yet the standard deviation was ₹5,571, more than twice the mean, and the single largest user accounted for 30 per cent of the entire sample's spend. Dropping the three biggest accounts moved the mean from ₹2,554.50 to ₹1,164.32, a fall of 54 per cent, while the median moved only from ₹965 to ₹910. The trimmed mean of ₹1,438.89 sat between the two. Exhibit 2 and its chart show the same thing by spend band.

Gayatri read Exhibit 2 twice. Over half the users spent under ₹1,000, and the last five users, 12.5 per cent of the sample, produced 65.6 per cent of the money. "The average user" described no one in the room. The nearest actual person to ₹2,555 was a user who paid ₹2,400, and only two users spent within ₹500 of it (₹2,100 and ₹2,400).

4. The people

Girish Vaze, chief financial officer, Mumbai, wants a ceiling he can defend. He is a careful man who has twice been embarrassed by marketing promises that outran provisions, and he will accept a lower launch ambition in exchange for a number that does not move after the board meets.

Gurinder Vig, head of growth, Singapore, wants a headline that sells. "One per cent on every bill" is clean, quotable and fits a banner. He regards any cap as a footnote that customers will read as a betrayal and argues that rivals such as PhonePe and Paytm will shout their own festive offers just as loudly.

Gauri Venugopal, data scientist, Toronto, wants nobody to build on 40 rows what ought to be built on 1,20,000. She has said plainly that the full-base pull needs a backfill from UPI reconciliation files and will not finish before 21 October.

Gunjan Vellore, designer, Berlin, is working on the offer screen. She wants to show each user a monthly "you earned" figure and is uneasy that the typical user would see about ₹10 while the headline invites expectations of far more. Her view of fairness is simple: show people what they will actually get.

5. The cost question

The disagreement is, at bottom, about which statistic answers which question. If the question is "what does a typical Gold user experience?", the median of ₹965 answers it: 1 per cent of that is ₹9.65, barely above the old flat ₹10. If the question is "what will the whole programme cost?", the answer depends on total spend, and total spend is the mean times the number of users. A median-based budget would give 1,20,000 × ₹9.65, or ₹11.58 lakh a month, and would understate the bill by well over half, because the five big spenders are real money and not noise. The mean gives 1,20,000 × ₹25.545, or ₹30.65 lakh a month.

Gauri added a caution that cut the other way. With 40 observations and a standard deviation of ₹5,571, the standard error of the mean is ₹880.81 (5,570.73 divided by the square root of 40). A conventional 95 per cent interval, using the t value of 2.0227 for 39 degrees of freedom, runs from about ₹773 to ₹4,336. Applied to the whole base, that is a monthly cost of roughly ₹9.27 lakh to ₹52.03 lakh. She also warned that such an interval assumes a roughly symmetric distribution, which this one plainly is not, so the true uncertainty is, if anything, understated. The point estimate is right in principle and fragile in practice.

Exhibit 3 shows why the cap matters more than its small effect on the typical user suggests. The user at the median receives ₹9.65 under either rule; the cap changes nothing for 38 of the 40 sampled users. It changes the programme's worst case, though, and the worst case lives entirely in the tail that nobody has measured well.

6. The options

Option A: approve 1 per cent uncapped and budget at the mean. The ceiling would be ₹30.65 lakh a month. The upside is the clean headline Gurinder wants and no friction in the offer screen. The cost is exposure: if the sample's tail is heavier than the base's, or if the offer itself draws large payers who were previously using other apps, the real bill could approach the top of Gauri's range, and it has no ceiling to stop it.

Option B: approve 1 per cent with a ₹100 monthly cap and budget at ₹21.80 lakh. The upside is a bounded downside and a lower provision for Girish; the typical user is unaffected. The cost is a footnote on the banner, a risk of upsetting the big payers whom Lekhni most wants to keep, and a budget that still rests on two sampled users above the cap.

Option C: defer the ceiling and launch date until the full-base data is in. Gauri's pull would replace 40 rows with 1,20,000 and settle the argument. The cost is time: sign-off would move to about 23 October and the launch to the end of the month, which cuts into the pre-Diwali window, and the board may read the delay as indecision.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1b, which statistic best describes the typical Gold user, and which best predicts total programme cost? Why are they different, and why does it matter that five of the 40 users are so far from the rest?

2. In Exhibit 2, what share of users and what share of spend sit in the top band? How would a reader be misled by presenting only the ₹2,555 average on a slide for the board?

3. Exhibit 3 scales a 40-user sample to a 1,20,000-user base. What would you want to know about how the sample was drawn, and how much weight should the ₹8.85 lakh cap saving carry?

4. Which option would you take to the board on Friday, and what would you say if Girish asks how confident you are in the number?

8. A note for the learner

This case is a lesson in choosing the statistic to fit the question. A median describes a typical case and resists outliers; a mean describes totals and is dragged by them. Budgets are made of totals, so the mean is the correct basis for a cost ceiling even though it fits no real user, but a mean from a sample this skewed is an unstable estimate, and the standard deviation larger than the mean is the warning sign. Always look at the shape before choosing the summary: sort the data, find the quartiles, and ask what happens when the top few are removed.

One defensible path is a hybrid of options B and C. Ask Girish to approve a ceiling of ₹21.80 lakh a month on the capped rule, labelled as provisional, with an explicit trigger: if the full-base pull due on 21 October shows a full-base cost above ₹30 lakh on the capped rule, a 38 per cent overrun on ₹21.80 lakh (the uncapped sample estimate of ₹30.65 lakh sits just above that line, which is deliberate) or a tail share materially different from the sample's, return to the board before launch on 26 October. This keeps the launch date, gives the finance team a bounded commitment, tells the truth to users through Gunjan's offer screen, and treats the sample as what it is, an early read. It also lets Gurinder keep a simple headline: "1% back, up to ₹100 a month". The weaker answers are the median-based budget, which understates cost by more than half, and the uncapped mean, which is correct in expectation and has no protection if it is wrong.
case40v1-q.stats.basics:
Indian School of Business · Software Product Management · Case 40

Mapan Commerce Technologies: Sixteen Minutes

Bengaluru, Sunday 18 October 2026. A quick-commerce operator has reported the same number for thirty-one months. The number is arithmetically correct and almost nobody in the company now believes it means what they thought it meant.

1. The night before

The lights on the fourth floor of Mapan Commerce Technologies' office on Bannerghatta Road were still on at a quarter to eleven on Sunday night. Hemangi Apte, Senior Director of Product, had the board deck open on one screen and, on the other, sixty numbers she had pulled herself from a logging pilot a month earlier. The deck said what it had said for two and a half years: average fulfilment time, 16.0 minutes, inside the sixteen-minute promise. The spreadsheet said that on one ordinary Saturday evening at one ordinary store, a quarter of the elapsed minutes had come from six orders out of sixty.

The board met at nine the next morning. The chief executive's Friday note had merged four items into one: whether to fund Promise 2.0, whether to reprice Mapan Plus, whether to close four stores in the National Capital Region, and what to say to Manara Grocers Group in Dubai, whose auditors had written on 2 October that Mapan was in breach of its service-level undertaking. Each item had an owner, and each owner had a different answer from what they insisted was the same data.

Hemangi had spent the weekend trying to write one slide that could hold all four, and had failed. What she had instead was a conviction that the four questions were downstream of a fifth that nobody had put on the agenda: what, exactly, the company had been measuring since March 2024, and over which population. Her last draft of that slide had been a single sentence, and she had deleted it because she could not decide whether it was a confession or an insight.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Mapan was founded in Hyderabad in August 2022 by Haresh Avasthi and two classmates from the College of Engineering, Pune, on a thesis that Indian quick commerce would be won on consistency rather than speed. It operated dark stores — small, high-turn neighbourhood warehouses — selling groceries for delivery in minutes. By October 2026 it ran 183 stores across Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Pune and the NCR and had raised a Series C of ₹620 crore from Mahanadi Growth Partners in February 2025 at a post-money valuation of ₹4,100 crore.

In March 2024, before the first store in Bengaluru opened, Mapan made a decision that it has not been able to unmake. The company adopted a public sixteen-minute promise, and — because the engineering team needed a definition it could compute cheaply every night from a store-level rollup — defined the metric as the mean of the monthly average fulfilment times of all live stores. Hrishikesh Anvekar, then the second engineer and now VP Engineering, wrote the job in an afternoon. It was correct, cheap, and it treated a store with 3,480 orders in a month exactly as it treated a store with 21,450.

Two consequences followed, neither visible at the time. The first was commercial: when Mapan licensed the stack to Manara Grocers Group of Dubai in August 2025, the master licence imported the 2024 definition verbatim into the service-level schedule. The second was architectural: because the nightly rollup was all anyone needed, per-order records were never persisted — the pipeline aggregated to store-day level before anything reached disk. Mapan therefore cannot reconstruct the distribution of its delivery times for any month before September 2026. It has thirty-one months of means and almost nothing else.

3. The industry

By late 2026 Indian quick commerce was no longer a land grab. Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart held most of the metro volume; BigBasket and DMart Ready held the planned weekly basket; Flipkart Minutes and JioMart pressed on price and on reach into tier-two cities. Contribution per order was measured in rupees, not hundreds of rupees, and the marginal customer was increasingly a tier-two household for whom a ₹199 membership was a considered purchase.

Regulation shaped the edges. Mapan's membership was collected through UPI autopay mandates under the National Payments Corporation of India's framework, and an e-mandate is authorised up to a cap: Mapan could reduce the ₹199 quarterly charge at will, but could not raise it without fresh authorisation from every member. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act meant the consumer panel Mapan had commissioned could not be joined to individual order histories without a specific consent the vendor had not collected. FSSAI licensing governed the cold chain, GST applied to the membership fee, and ONDC was making the catalogue comparable to competitors' in ways Mapan could not control.

Mapan's global exposure ran through two channels. The licensing business, run out of Edison, New Jersey, sold the promise stack to grocery operators outside India; Manara in Dubai was by far the largest, at an annual licence fee of ₹14.5 crore renewable on 31 March 2027. The product organisation was itself distributed: engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, a principal designer in Berlin, the lead data scientist in Toronto, customer success in Singapore. The design review ran at 12.30 p.m. India time, so Berlin could attend before lunch and Toronto could not.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence matters, because at each point the company believed something that it no longer believes.

Through 2024 and 2025 the nightly job reported between 15.4 and 16.1 minutes, and the company treated it as settled. Late-delivery tickets ran at a low, stable rate and were attributed to monsoon and to riders. In March 2026 Mapan opened eleven stores in the NCR in nine weeks and held the sixteen-minute promise in its advertising there, because the nightly figure stayed inside sixteen. In June 2026 it printed 16.0 while NCR complaints rose by what Haripriya Attavar's team called “not a step change, a slope”.

Per-order logging had been running at MP-HYD-07 in Kukatpally since 5 September 2026 as a single-store trial. On 12 September, Hiranmayi Ajrekar extended it to eleven more stores — three in Hyderabad, three in Bengaluru, two in Pune and four in the NCR, twelve in all across four cities — but in a lighter form: those eleven ship a nightly summary of counts, mean, median and percentiles, not the per-order rows themselves. Her stated purpose was to build a per-order prediction model. What the logs produced first was a description. Exhibit 1 is the September output. Two numbers in it had not been seen inside the company before: the order-weighted average fulfilment time, and the ninetieth percentile.

On the evening of Saturday 19 September, Hemangi pulled every order dispatched from store MP-HYD-07 in Kukatpally between 7 p.m. and 10 p.m. — sixty orders — and sorted them by hand. That list is Exhibit 2. On 2 October, Manara's audit — which measures elapsed time from picker-accept, not from order placement — filed a notice asserting breach. On 6 October, Hoshedar Asrani's team circulated a renewal deck containing a retention chart; re-cut by Hiranmayi on 9 October, it became Exhibits 3a and 3b. On 10 October the August panel arrived and contradicted the price research on which the ₹199 membership had been set. Those are Exhibits 4 and 5.

5. The people

Hemangi Apte — Senior Director, Product, Bengaluru
Owns the promise. Position: the promise should become a per-order predicted window rather than a single number, which means funding Promise 2.0. Incentive: her promotion case rests on Promise 2.0 shipping this financial year. Not saying: she approved the NCR launch on the strength of the nightly figure without asking how it was computed, and the board may work that out on Monday.
Haresh Avasthi — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Bengaluru
Position: the sixteen-minute promise is the brand and must not be touched before the Series D conversations in the first quarter of 2027. Incentive: valuation. Not saying: Mahanadi's partner has already asked him, informally, what Mapan's p90 is, and he did not know.
Hrishikesh Anvekar — VP Engineering, Pune
Position: the metric is defensible, the data retention policy was correct at the time, and Promise 2.0 at ₹6.4 crore is a rebuild of a system that works. Incentive: his team's roadmap is already committed to a catalogue migration. Not saying: he wrote the 2024 definition, and he has known since June that the weighting was wrong, having mentioned it once in a thread that nobody answered.
Hiranmayi Ajrekar — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto
Position: the company should report the median and the ninetieth percentile and stop reporting the mean. Incentive: her credibility rests on the pilot she built. Not saying: her stratified re-cut of the membership data (Exhibit 3b) rests on a “heavy user” definition she chose after seeing the result, and the DPDP consent position means she cannot validate it against the panel.
Haripriya Attavar — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Position: customers complain about variance, not the average — the same household gets eleven minutes on Tuesday and thirty-eight on Saturday. Incentive: her contact-rate target. Not saying: her team's tagging taxonomy changed in May 2026, so the rise in late-delivery tickets is partly reclassification and she does not know how much.
Hoshedar Asrani — SVP Global Licensing, Edison, New Jersey
Position: do not reopen the SLA definition; fix the four slow NCR stores quietly and report the same metric. Incentive: the Manara renewal is 61 per cent of his annual quota. Not saying: he has already shown Manara the membership retention chart as evidence that Mapan's stack drives loyalty.
Hemakshi Aiyangar — Principal Designer, Berlin
Position: a predicted window of “12–19 minutes” reads as a hedge to Indian customers and will be tested as weakness; a single number is a promise, a range is an excuse. Incentive: she is judged on the app's conversion funnel. Not saying: her own usability sessions in Pune showed that customers given a range were more satisfied when the order was late and less satisfied when it was early.
Harshvardhan Amdekar — Chief Operating Officer, Manara Grocers Group, Dubai
Position: the licence promises sixteen minutes and his stores do not deliver it. Incentive: he is renegotiating his own group's rider contracts and a supplier breach strengthens him. Not saying: Manara's measurement starts at picker-accept, which excludes an average of 2.4 minutes of queueing, and his team has never shared the raw logs.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the document that started the argument, and it can be read in three ways. Count each store once down the Avg minutes column and the answer is 16.0 minutes: the company is inside its promise. Weight each store by the orders it served and the answer is 18.08 minutes, because three of the four slowest stores in the table are also among the four largest. Read the right-hand columns instead and the answer is that in the NCR more than a quarter of orders breach, 13,882 orders of 51,430, and that the ninetieth percentile at Gurugram is 43 minutes, more than two and a half times the promise.

Figure C is the picture Hiranmayi has asked the board to look at instead of the number. The mode sits at thirteen minutes and the median at fourteen; the mean sits at eighteen, pulled there almost entirely by six orders. Strip those six and the remaining fifty-four averaged 14.56 minutes. Haripriya's argument is that no household experiences 18.00 minutes — they get thirteen minutes most Tuesdays and sixty-eight once, and it is the sixty-eight that reaches X and the Play Store review that drags the rating.

7. Voices

“We have reported this number every month for thirty-one months. Investors have it. Customers have it on hoardings in Kukatpally. If we stand up on Monday and say the real number is eighteen, we are not correcting a metric, we are retracting a promise. And we will be asked when we knew.”

Haresh Avasthi, chief executive, in the Friday pre-read call

“The number is not wrong. It is the mean of the store means, and that is exactly what it says it is. If you want a different number, specify a different number. What you cannot do is tell me in October 2026 that the definition I was given in March 2024 was a mistake, and also tell me that rebuilding it is not a priority because of the catalogue migration.”

Hrishikesh Anvekar, VP Engineering, Pune, in the metrics thread

“I keep being asked which one is correct. Both are. They answer different questions. The store mean answers ‘how is a typical store doing’; the order-weighted mean answers ‘how is a typical order doing’. Customers place orders, not stores. But if you want the number that predicts a complaint, it is neither. It is the ninetieth percentile.”

Hiranmayi Ajrekar, lead data scientist, Toronto, 9 October, 07.12 IST

“Please do not send Manara a second definition. Harshvardhan will take any change as an admission and reprice the renewal. Fix the four stores. The metric will follow.”

Hoshedar Asrani, SVP Global Licensing, Edison, email to Hemangi Apte, 7 October

“Our tickets do not say ‘your average is too high’. They say ‘yesterday it came in nine minutes and today it is thirty-four and I have guests’. The complaint is about the spread, not the centre. I have been saying this since April and I have been given a mean every month.”

Haripriya Attavar, head of customer success, Singapore, in the October business review

“A range is not a promise. In Pune the customers who were shown ‘12–19 minutes’ rated us higher when we were late and lower when we were early. I am not sure that is a win. We would be buying forgiveness for our worst days by giving up credit for our best ones.”

Hemakshi Aiyangar, principal designer, Berlin, design review, 14 October

“My stores are not getting sixteen minutes. Your schedule says sixteen minutes. I do not need to agree with your statistics to invoke a clause.”

Harshvardhan Amdekar, COO, Manara Grocers Group, Dubai, call of 9 October

8. The options as Hemangi currently sees them

One: fund Promise 2.0. Replace the single promise with a per-order predicted window computed at checkout, and report the median and the ninetieth percentile internally. Cost ₹6.40 crore over two quarters — twenty-two engineers in Bengaluru and Pune at ₹5.28 crore of fully loaded cost, and ₹1.12 crore of cloud and model infrastructure. It delays the catalogue migration by a quarter. It also requires telling Manara that the metric in its schedule was the wrong one.

Two: hold the promise, fix the stores. Close or rebuild the three NCR stores that Exhibit 1 puts above nineteen minutes — Gurugram Sector 49, Delhi Rohini and Noida Sector 62. Hoshedar Asrani's email of 7 October says “the four stores”, and Friday's agenda repeated it; but the fourth of the pilot's four slowest is Bengaluru Whitefield, not an NCR store, and the fourth NCR pilot store, Faridabad NIT, is one of the fastest in the fleet. Nobody has corrected the count. Exhibit 6 says the NCR lost ₹0.86 crore of contribution in the quarter, so the financial case is easy; what is not easy is that NCR is 21.5 lakh of the quarter's 78.0 lakh orders, and the Series D story is national coverage.

Three: reopen the Manara definition. Offer an order-weighted mean prospectively, accept the penalty of ₹1.16 crore for the quarter in dispute — eight per cent of the ₹14.5 crore annual fee — and attempt to keep the 31 March renewal. Hoshedar believes this loses the renewal and with it the licensing thesis.

Four: reprice Mapan Plus to ₹149. Exhibit 5 says ₹149 raises more from a thousand respondents than ₹199 does. The UPI mandate rules allow a reduction without re-authorisation and forbid an increase without it, so this door opens once and does not close.

Hemangi had written all four on a single page and then written underneath, in the margin: all four of these assume the problem is the promise. Nobody had asked whether the unit of analysis should be the order, the customer or the store-week; whether a household that gets thirteen minutes four times and thirty-eight once is satisfied or angry; or what it means that the only distribution Mapan possesses is three hours long and came from one store on one Saturday, chosen because the logging happened to be on.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday 19 October 2026. Cash at 30 September was ₹389 crore; the plan for the four quarters beginning 1 October 2026 burns ₹62 crore a quarter, giving a little over six quarters of runway to roughly the end of April 2028, and Mahanadi will not lead a Series D without national coverage or a credible unit-economics turn. Havovi Agashe, the chief financial officer, has told Hemangi that ₹6.40 crore is available this year but only once, and that she will not fund Promise 2.0 and a market exit in the same cycle.

The Manara licence gives Mapan thirty days from 2 October to respond to the breach notice, which expires on 1 November. Per-order rows exist for one store and six weeks; nightly summaries exist for twelve stores and one month; everything before September 2026 is store-month averages and cannot be re-derived. The panel cannot be linked to order histories without fresh DPDP consent, which Mitrika estimates at six weeks and ₹34 lakh. Membership prices can be cut unilaterally and never raised. And the hoardings in Kukatpally, Whitefield and Sector 49 are booked through the festive quarter.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using only Exhibit 2, state the mean, median, mode, interquartile range and ninetieth percentile, and say which of them you would put on a slide for the chief executive and which for the head of customer success. Defend the difference.
  2. Exhibit 1 supports both 16.0 minutes and 18.08 minutes. Identify precisely what population each figure averages over, and say which population the sixteen-minute promise was made to.
  3. Exhibit 3a reports a 24.1-point retention advantage for Mapan Plus and Exhibit 3b reduces it to about 5 points. What would you need to observe — and what would you need to run — before telling the board that membership causes retention? What does footnote (iii) of Exhibit 3b do to your confidence?
  4. Exhibits 4 and 5 come from the same thousand people and disagree about ₹199. Reconcile them if you can. If you cannot, decide which you would price on, and state what you are assuming about the people who said ₹0.
  5. Haripriya Attavar argues that variance, not the mean, is what customers experience. Design the single metric you would report monthly to the board, and show what it would have said in September 2026 using only the data in the exhibits. What does your metric hide?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Hemangi Apte do before nine o'clock, what does she say to the board about a number the company has published for thirty-one months, and what does she say to Harshvardhan Amdekar on the call at two? If she has to choose between being right about the statistics and keeping the Manara renewal, which does she choose, and what does that choice commit Mapan to for the next two years?

At twenty past eleven Hemangi closed the deck and opened the sixty numbers again. She tried reading them as a customer would: thirteen, thirteen, fourteen, fourteen — and then, somewhere down the column, sixty-eight. She thought about the household at the end of that row, on a Saturday evening in Kukatpally, waiting an hour and eight minutes for a promise of sixteen, and about the fact that it appeared in the company's reporting as one-sixtieth of one store's evening, in a store that was one of twelve in the pilot and one of 183 in the fleet, folded into a number that was itself the wrong number. She did not know whether she had found a metrics bug, a product failure, or the ordinary cost of running 183 stores in four Indian cities. She had nine hours to decide, and she had not yet written the slide.
exp40v2-q.stats.basics:
Descriptive statistics for PMs

Near-expert reading. Do I know enough statistics to avoid being fooled by an average or a correlation?

1. Two decisions, three days apart

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, in a filling hall outside Nashik, Mandar Belapurkar had a costed proposal he could not argue with. As head of product and category at Lavangi Foods Industries, he owned a 200 g millet-and-sattu mix: 84 lakh pouches in the year to March 2026 at a net realisation of ₹96 a pouch, or ₹80.64 crore. Two filler lines, L and M, both ran to a target of 202 g. Finance had costed those two extra grams: 2 g on 84 lakh pouches is 16,800 kg of mix, and at ₹420 a kilogram that is ₹70.56 lakh a year, 22.1 per cent of the ₹3.20 crore the line earned in EBITDA. Reset both lines to 200.8 g, the paper said.

His quality lead Mythili Raghavendra, in Coimbatore, had weighed twelve consecutive pouches from each line that morning. Both samples averaged exactly 202.0 g. Her note read: “The averages are identical and the lines are not.”

Three days later, on Friday 9 October, Lavanika Sohoni read a board pack in Bengaluru. As vice-president of product at Mapan Quality Labs, which sells inspection software to 312 mid-size factories, she had two numbers before her: an average annual contract value of ₹10.0 lakh, from which finance had built a forecast of ₹31.20 crore, and a correlation of 0.981 between inspections logged per seat per week and net revenue retention, from which growth had derived a roadmap — build nudges, lift logging, lift retention. The two decisions look unrelated and are the same decision. A descriptive statistic is a choice about what to discard, and the only test of it is whether the discarded part mattered to the decision in hand. Mapan's board had the right statistic for the wrong question; Lavangi's finance team had the right question and the wrong feature of the distribution.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Descriptive statistics are functionals of a finite set of observations: one number computed from many, chosen to preserve a single property and indifferent to the rest. The mean preserves the total, the median rank, the variance squared dispersion. None preserves the data, which is the point.

The lineage runs from John Graunt's bills of mortality in 1662 through Adolphe Quetelet's homme moyen of 1835, the first serious claim that an average describes a person, to Karl Pearson, who named the “standard deviation” in 1894 and, on Francis Galton's work on heredity, formalised the correlation coefficient in 1896. Ronald Fisher named the variance in 1918; Walter Shewhart drew the first control chart in 1924, insisting that variation and not level was the subject. Then the correctives: Edward Simpson in 1951 on the reversal that bears his name, W. S. Robinson on the ecological fallacy in 1950, Peter Huber on robust estimation in 1964, John Tukey on exploring data before modelling it, and Anscombe's quartet of 1973 — four datasets with identical means, variances and correlations and nothing else in common.

Four positions survive, and their holders argue. The parametric school treats the mean and standard deviation as the sufficient statistics of an assumed distribution; it signs “report the mean, the standard deviation and the model behind them” but not “the median is the safe default”, since under a good model the median discards information. The robust and exploratory school replies that business data is never well specified: “resistance beats efficiency on real ledgers”, yes; “the standard deviation is a safe summary of money”, no. The quality-engineering school signs “a mean without its spread is not a measurement” but not “remove the outliers”, because to Shewhart the outlier is the signal. The decision-theoretic school holds that the loss function picks the statistic — squared loss the mean, absolute loss the median, threshold loss a tail probability.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Conventions first, because expert disagreement is often convention mismatch. The variance here is the sample variance, dividing summed squared deviations by n − 1; percentiles use linear interpolation between order statistics, the default in NumPy and R's type 7.

The fourteen values in Exhibit 1 sum to ₹140.0 lakh, so the mean is exactly ₹10.0 lakh; the seventh and eighth sorted values are 4.1 and 4.5, so the median is ₹4.3 lakh. The deviations from 10.0 sum to zero, as they must, and their squares sum to 3,173.06, which over thirteen degrees of freedom gives a variance of 244.08 and a standard deviation of ₹15.62 lakh. That exceeds the mean: the coefficient of variation is 1.56. The largest account, ₹61.0 lakh of the ₹140.0 lakh sampled, is 43.6 per cent of the total alone; the top three are ₹95.0 lakh of ₹140.0 lakh, or 67.9 per cent. Three of fourteen lie above the mean, 21.4 per cent; seven of fourteen above the median, 50.0 per cent by construction.

The mean is not wrong at Mapan; it is the only right statistic for the forecast, because a total is additive and the mean times the count reproduces it: ₹10.0 lakh across 312 accounts is ₹3,120 lakh, or ₹31.20 crore. Substitute the median and the same arithmetic gives ₹1,341.6 lakh, or ₹13.42 crore — short by ₹17.78 crore, 57.0 per cent of the mean-based figure. The second-order effect is that the standard deviation of a heavy-tailed sample estimates nothing stable. Of the 3,173.06 total squared deviation, the ₹61.0 lakh account alone contributes 2,601.00, which is 82.0 per cent. A coefficient of variation above 1 is the diagnostic: the spread is a property of whether the whale was drawn.

4. The conditions, stated so they can be tested

Claim one: the quantity is additive across rows. Then the mean is the statistic, being the total in disguise. True of Mapan's contract value and of Lavangi's giveaway — 2 g a pouch adds to 16,800 kg. False of anything already a ratio.

Claim two: the distribution has a scale. If doubling the sample leaves the standard deviation where it was, it means something. Lavangi's fill weights pass; Mapan's contract values fail at a coefficient of variation of 1.56.

Claim three: the decision has a threshold. Where money changes hands at a boundary — a statutory minimum weight, a support SLA, a credit cut-off — no measure of centre answers the question and a tail probability is required. Lavangi's decision is wholly of this kind, which is why a mean of 202.0 g was never relevant.

The idea turns misleading in the averaging of rates. Mapan's net revenue retention across the nine accounts with a full year of telemetry has an unweighted mean of 101.0 per cent; weighted by contract value, as retention must be, it is 109.72 per cent. The first belongs to a firm whose smallest customer matters as much as its largest.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product. Lavangi fills 200 g, 400 g and 1 kg packs. A grand mean of fill error across them is meaningless, because permitted tolerance scales with nominal weight; the comparable quantity is error as a proportion of declared weight — and even that hides the different machine.

Regulated. Indian packaged-commodity rules, administered through the states' legal metrology departments, combine an average-content requirement on a lot with a per-pack tolerance — two statistics on the same pouches, so a lot can pass the first while individual pouches fail the second. Lavangi's own rule, tighter than statute, is that no pouch may be more than 9 g below declared weight: a lower limit of 191 g. Compliance is a claim about a tail, and no central tendency discharges it.

Two-sided and platform. Mapan resells through four systems integrators. One ACV distribution across direct and resold accounts is a mixture of two populations with different price books, and a mixture's mean sits where neither lives.

Hardware plus software, and AI-native. A filler drifts within a shift as the hopper empties, so twelve consecutive pouches describe one moment, not the day. The AI analogue is the average eval score: a model at 94 per cent mean accuracy can be at 61 per cent on the slice that generates complaints.

At the organisational seams the pattern is consistent. Finance owns the mean because its statements are additive; quality owns the variance because its obligations are per-unit; product owns neither, inherits both, and is the only function that sees the decision whole.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The mean is a total, not a compromise

The tell is someone defending an average on grounds of typicality — “the average customer spends ₹10 lakh”. Experts hear a claim about addition and ask what is being added. The obvious reading, that the mean sits in the middle, fails for any skewed quantity: at Mapan it sits above eleven of the fourteen accounts.

Spread is usually the decision variable

The tell is two options presented as equivalent because their means match. Lavangi's lines are the canonical case: one mean, and only one line capable of the reset. Experts ask for spread before level, because level moves with a set point and spread does not.

A mean of rates is not a rate

The tell is a percentage column with a simple average at its foot and unequal bases above it. Mapan's 101.0 against 109.72 per cent gap is small enough to pass unnoticed and large enough to change a board's view of churn. The fix is a weighted mean with the base stated.

Rates compound and never average

Mapan's pilot funnel in the year to March 2026: of 2,500 plants contacted, 450 booked a pilot, 18.0 per cent; 198 of 450 converted to paid, 44.0 per cent; 165 of 198 were still paying a year on, 83.3 per cent. End to end, 165 of 2,500, or 6.6 per cent — exactly the product of the three. The mean of the three rates is 48.4 per cent, a figure with no referent that still reaches slides.

Percentile conventions disagree, so "p90" is not one number

By linear interpolation the 90th percentile of Exhibit 1 is ₹19.00 lakh; by nearest rank it is the thirteenth value, ₹22.0 lakh. The tell is two dashboards reporting different p90s from one table, and the cause is almost never a bug.

Aggregation inflates correlation

Correlate Mapan's nine telemetry accounts individually and r is 0.981; correlate the three size-band averages and r is 0.997. Averaging removes the within-group noise against which correlation should be tested. The tell is an r computed on segment means and quoted as if it described accounts.

Within-group relationships can reverse the pooled one

Mapan's pooled slope is 1.73 percentage points of retention per extra inspection; inside each size band the slope is 1.00 and r falls to 0.50. Size drives both variables, so the within-band slope is 58 per cent of the pooled one. Exhibit 7 is the harder version, where the ordering reverses outright.

The denominator is a choice, and zero is a value

“Average inspections per active account” is circular when activity is defined by inspecting. Experts insist the denominator be fixed before the metric is computed, and that accounts logging nothing enter the mean as zeros rather than vanish.

Small samples cannot resolve small tails

Twelve pouches can establish that line M is roughly twice as variable as line L. They cannot establish a breach rate of one in a thousand, which needs thousands of observations or an explicit distributional assumption. The tell is a capability index quoted to two decimals from a dozen measurements.

Identical summaries do not mean identical data

Anscombe's quartet is not a curiosity but the reason experts plot first. Lavangi's samples agree on the mean to the gram and disagree on all that matters. Before quoting a statistic, look at the rows.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products, spend is right-skewed and the median user is the one the roadmap serves, while the mean stays correct for infrastructure and payout budgets. In B2B and enterprise, Mapan's shape is typical: forecast on the mean, prioritise on a segmented median. In platforms and marketplaces, one average across two sides is meaningless. In hardware and physical goods, variance is the product: Lavangi's giveaway buys variance it has not removed. In AI products, the spread of errors across slices matters more than average error, because a user meets only their own slice.

Stage changes the risk, not the arithmetic. A team with 40 accounts should read the rows, since one row is a quarter of the picture. A growth-stage team should institutionalise percentiles before its dashboards harden. At scale the problem inverts: with lakhs of rows, trivial correlations become unmistakable, and the discipline becomes effect size.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Trim the tail, or keep it. The robust position is that one row contributing 82.0 per cent of the squared deviation makes every variance-based statistic a statement about that row, so trim and say so. The other position is that Mapan's ₹61.0 lakh account is not an error but 43.6 per cent of the sampled revenue, and that a trimmed mean of ₹6.44 lakh forecasts ₹20.10 crore against a billable ₹31.20 crore. The robust camp is wrong if the tail is the business; the trimmers are wrong if it is a data-entry artefact.

Standard deviation or interquartile range as the default. The parametric case is that the standard deviation feeds every downstream tool — capability indices, confidence intervals, control limits — and that Lavangi's decision is unmakeable without it. The exploratory case is that an interquartile range of ₹4.98 lakh describes Exhibit 1 honestly while ₹15.62 lakh describes nothing. It resolves only on whether a distributional model will be used.

May observational correlation ever justify a build? The experiment-only school says no: r of 0.981 pooled and 0.50 within bands are the same data, and only randomisation separates them. The causal-inference school answers that experiments are often impossible — Lavangi cannot randomise legal metrology — and that with a stated causal graph, matched comparisons and a sensitivity analysis, observational evidence can carry a decision. It is wrong if the unmeasured confounder is large; its opponents are wrong if waiting costs more than being misled.

Capability indices from small samples. Six Sigma practice computes an index from twenty or thirty measurements and acts on it. The Deming-descended position is that such an index is a distributional extrapolation masquerading as a measurement, and that one should chart the process and hunt assignable causes instead. Mandar's 1.16 and 0.51 are the contested object: useful as a ranking of two lines, indefensible as a prediction of parts per million.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this differs in three visible ways. They ask what decision a number is for before asking what it is. They report a centre, a spread and a count as one object. And they treat every correlation as a hypothesis with a named confounder, so the sentence is never “logging correlates with retention” but “… and size predicts both, so the test is a holdout within a band”.

12. What each of them decided

On Tuesday 20 October 2026, a fortnight after the filling-hall conversation, Mandar approved a split decision. Line L moves to 200.8 g at once, saving 1.2 g on 48 lakh pouches, or ₹24.19 lakh a year, while holding its breach rate at 97 pouches per lakh. Line M holds at 202 g until the ₹46 lakh filler is installed, because at 200.8 g it would breach at 8.594 per cent. The dashboard's headline became the share of pouches below 191 g, by line and volume-weighted.

Lavanika's decision was harder to sell. She kept the mean in the forecast: ₹31.20 crore stands, with the caveat that fourteen accounts cannot pin a mean driven by one row. She added the median of ₹4.3 lakh, the quartiles and the count above each to every roadmap document, reframing the typical customer from a ₹10.0 lakh account to a ₹4.3 lakh one. And she declined the nudges build on r of 0.981, commissioning a six-week holdout inside the mid-size band, where the slope is 1.00 rather than 1.73. Her note ran to one line: a correlation tells you what has happened together; only an intervention tells you what will happen next.

Three questions for discussion. First: the giveaway is ₹70.56 lakh a year and the filler costs ₹46 lakh; if the board declines the capex, what is the defensible target weight for line M? Second: had Manjiri's sample excluded the largest account, the mean and the forecast would both have fallen — what procedure keeps a forecast from depending on whether the whale was drawn? Third: who should own the choice between Exhibit 7's pooled and within-channel readings?

13. Going deeper

Significance, power, sample size and peeking says how far fourteen accounts or twelve pouches can be trusted, and makes Lavanika's holdout designable. Sampling and representativeness precedes everything here: Manjiri's random draw is the only reason a mean of ₹10.0 lakh estimates anything. Statistical segmentation turns Exhibit 5's size bands into a defensible partition. Survey design matters because most PM data is self-reported. Quantitative concept testing applies these summaries before behavioural data exists, and conjoint and MaxDiff extend them to trade-offs. NPS, CSAT and CES are the discipline's most abused descriptive statistics, and the mean-of-rates nuance is the key to them. The Sean Ellis PMF survey is one proportion read as a threshold. Consumer panels and syndicated data supply category distributions a ledger cannot. Model metrics: precision, recall and AUC carry tail reasoning into classifiers, where mean accuracy is the mean fill weight of the AI era.

Descriptive statistics for PMs

Question answered: do I know enough statistics to avoid being fooled by an average or a correlation?

1. The number on the board slide

On Thursday 8 October 2026, Ishani Lonkar, group product manager at Inaam Rewards Exchange, had forty minutes before the quarterly review and two figures to check. Inaam, a Mumbai company, runs a points marketplace on which about 1,10,000 monthly active users earn points at partner merchants and redeem them for vouchers. The chief executive wanted to launch a premium tier, Swarn Club, offering five per cent extra cashback to "above-average" redeemers, on a reward budget of ₹60 lakh a quarter. The slide read: "Average monthly redemption per user: ₹800. Threshold for Swarn Club: ₹800."

The second figure came from the growth team. Over eight weeks starting 10 August, notifications per user per week had risen and so had the redemption rate, and the correlation between them was 0.87. The proposal was to raise notifications from the current average of 5.5 a week to nine.

Isaac Thekkekara, an analyst in Kochi, had pulled eleven users at random from September's ledger, and Ajinkya Phadnis, a data engineer in Pune, had sent the rows. Exhibit 1 shows them. Only one of the eleven would qualify for the tier. At ₹800 the flagship benefit would reach roughly one user in eleven, and the notification plan rested on a correlation that coincided with the festive season. Both errors came from treating a summary as if it were the data.

2. The idea

Descriptive statistics are numbers that summarise a set of observations: where they centre, how widely they scatter, and whether two measurements move together. Unlike inferential statistics, which ask whether a sample's pattern holds in the wider population, they only describe the rows in hand. The toolkit solves an old problem. Once a body of records is too large to read, someone must compress it, and every compression discards information. Descriptive statistics are the disciplined ways of choosing what to discard.

The lineage is short. Gauss and Legendre developed least squares around 1800; Francis Galton in the 1880s noticed that tall parents have tall but less extreme children; Karl Pearson formalised the correlation coefficient and the term "standard deviation" in the 1890s.

The sentence Ishani could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib was this: "An average tells you where the total would sit if everyone were equal; it does not tell you where anyone actually is."

3. How it works

Three questions cover nearly all practical use. First, where is the centre? The mean is the sum of all values divided by their count. The median is the middle value once the rows are sorted, or the midpoint of the two middle values if the count is even. Second, how wide is the scatter? The standard deviation measures the typical distance of a value from the mean. The steps are the ones practitioners often leave implicit: subtract the mean from every value, square each deviation so that negatives cannot cancel positives, add the squares, divide by the count less one (for a sample), and take the square root to return to rupees. Third, do two measures move together? The correlation coefficient, r, multiplies each pair's deviations from the two means, adds them, and divides by the square root of the product of the two sums of squared deviations. It lies between -1 and +1.

In Exhibit 1 the rows sum to ₹8,800, so the mean of eleven is ₹800. Sorted, the sixth of eleven values is ₹270, the median. The two "averages" differ by a factor of almost three, and the reason is visible: one user, at ₹6,100, accounts for 69.3 per cent of the total. She is a corporate gifting account; the other ten hold ₹2,700, or 30.7 per cent.

Figure 1 deserves a slow read. The ten dots sit on one short axis, with the median (dashed) and the mean (solid) almost on top of one another at 260 and 270. The arrow on the right is the whole argument: one point outside the frame moves the mean by hundreds of rupees and the median by ten.

4. A worked example, line by line

Begin with the ten ordinary users. Their sum is 140 + 180 + 210 + 230 + 250 + 270 + 290 + 320 + 360 + 450 = 2,700, so the mean is ₹270. Sorted, the fifth and sixth values are 250 and 270, so the median is their midpoint, ₹260. Exhibit 2 then subtracts 270 from each value. The deviations total exactly zero, a property of the mean and a useful check, and the squared deviations total 74,000.

5. Nuances worth knowing

The mean and the median answer different questions

The mean answers "what would each user get if the total were shared equally?" That suits budgeting, where rupees are fungible. The median answers "what does the user in the middle experience?" That suits decisions about typical behaviour.

Skew is the rule in money data

Spend and order value are bounded below by zero and unbounded above, so a few large values stretch the right tail. When the mean sits well above the median, as in Exhibit 1a, the distribution is right-skewed. Report both numbers, and use percentiles (the 25th, 50th, 90th) to describe the tail.

Spread needs its own number

Two products can share a mean of ₹270 yet differ completely: in one every user is near it, in the other half are near zero. As a habit, when the standard deviation exceeds the mean, stop and plot the data.

Outliers are information, not just noise

Deleting user 11 gives tidy statistics, but she is a real account with a real redemption cost, and a corporate segment may deserve its own product. Report with and without her, and say which question each answer serves.

Correlation measures linear association only

Pearson's r detects straight-line relationships. A relationship that rises and then falls, such as engagement against notifications once users start muting the app, can give an r near zero. Nor does r state a slope: 0.87 is not an 87 per cent effect.

Correlation is not causation, and the third variable is usually the culprit

Two measures can rise together because a third drives both. Exhibit 3 contains exactly this trap. Across all eight weeks r is 0.873. In the five ordinary weeks, notifications rose from 2 to 6 a week and the redemption rate stayed flat at about 4.2 per cent, with r of only 0.139.

The fitted slope across all eight weeks is about 0.53 percentage points per extra notification; across the first five it is 0.01.

A small sample cannot be forgiven by good arithmetic

Eleven users, or eight weeks, are teaching examples. Correct arithmetic on them still says little about 1,10,000 users; how precisely a sample estimates a population is the business of significance, power and sample size.

6. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products such as Inaam, behaviour is heavily skewed and the median user is the one the roadmap serves. In B2B products, a handful of enterprise accounts can account for most of the revenue, so the mean per account is dominated by a few contracts; analysts there habitually segment by account size before computing anything. In a marketplace, a single average across buyers and sellers is usually meaningless, because a thousand casual buyers and ten professional sellers need separate distributions, and supply and demand move together for structural reasons.

Stage matters too. An early-stage company with a few hundred users should simply read the individual rows, since one user changes the picture. A large company has the opposite problem: huge samples make tiny correlations look unmistakable, so the discipline lies in asking whether an effect is big enough to matter.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting the mean of a skewed measure as "the typical user." The symptom is a headline average that no customer in a sample resembles, as with the ₹800 on the board slide. The mean is the centre of the rupees, not of the people. The cheapest diagnostic is the median beside it; if they differ by more than a fifth, plot the data.

Reading r as proof of a lever. The symptom is a proposal to turn a dial because it "correlates" with the goal. The misunderstanding is that association implies intervention. The diagnostic is to split by time or segment, as Exhibit 3 does, and see whether the relationship survives.

Trimming outliers without saying so. The symptom is a metric that improves after a data clean; the diagnostic is to publish the excluded count and the metric both ways.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Ishani's morning would have put a small distribution on the slide rather than one figure: the median (₹270), the mean (₹800), the standard deviation, and the share of users above each candidate threshold. It would have stated the sample size and shown that the gifting account carries 69.3 per cent of the sampled rupees. For the notification claim, it would have shown the two periods separately, a flat line before the festival and a steep one after, and proposed a small holdout test rather than a rollout.

9. What Ishani decided

She replaced the slide. The Swarn Club threshold moved from ₹800 to the median, with the full-population median to be recomputed from all 1,10,000 users before launch; in the sample that threshold admits five of eleven users, or 45.5 per cent, and corporate accounts were routed to a separate programme. She declined to endorse the nine-a-week plan on the strength of r of 0.873, and instead asked Isaac for a four-week test holding some users at five and a half notifications a week while others received more. Her reasoning: data could describe what had happened, but only an experiment could show what a change would cause.

Next to learn: significance, power and sample size, which say how far an eleven-row observation can be trusted.

Two questions to sit with. If your product's headline metric is an average, what is its median, and what does the gap tell you about who you are building for? And which of your favourite correlations would survive being split into the weeks before and after something else changed?

Survey design: writing a survey whose answers you can believe

1. A number the board liked too much

On the morning of 21 August 2026, Gunwant Ketkar, head of consumer research at Gulal Paints Network, opened a spreadsheet and saw a figure he did not trust. Gulal sells interior and exterior paints through dealers across India and, increasingly, through a mobile app that lets homeowners book colour consultations. Competing against incumbents such as Asian Paints and Berger, it had spent a year developing a premium ten-year waterproofing coat. The company would stock it only if enough customers would pay a premium for it. The chief financial officer, Girdhari Mathur, had set the bar plainly: the product needed at least 35 per cent of buyers choosing it over the standard coat for the ₹18 crore inventory and dealer-display commitment to break even.

The survey had gone to 2,50,000 app users. The headline, prepared by an analyst in Lagos, Ogechi Eze, read that 71 per cent of respondents agreed the premium coat was worth paying extra for. Girdhari wanted to sign the commitment that afternoon. Gunwant hesitated because he had written the question himself, in a hurry, and he could now see its wording in his mind: How much do you agree that a coat that protects your home for ten years is worth paying extra for?

If the 71 per cent was real, Gulal would commit ₹18 crore to a winner. If it was an artefact of wording and of who chose to answer, the company would carry unsold tins into the monsoon of 2027. The decision was a narrow one: how much of this number was measurement, and how much was manufactured by the instrument?

2. The idea

A survey is a structured set of questions put to a sample of people, designed so that the answers can be counted and generalised to a larger group, called the population. Survey design is the discipline of making sure that the counted answers mean what you think they mean. It covers who is asked (the sample), what is asked and in what words, in what order, and on what response scale.

The discipline exists because respondents do not read off a stored opinion the way a clerk reads a ledger. Cognitive psychologists working on survey methodology, notably Norman Bradburn, Seymour Sudman and Norbert Schwarz from the 1970s onward, showed that people construct an answer on the spot, using whatever the question puts in front of them: its wording, its earlier items, its offered options. A survey is less like a thermometer than a conversation, and conversations steer. Questions that steer the answer toward one response are called leading. The craft is to remove the steering you can control and to measure the rest.

The sentence Gunwant could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: a survey result is only as believable as the worst of three things, namely whether the people who answered resemble the people we care about, whether the question lets them say no, and whether we can show how the number moves when we change the instrument.

3. How it actually works

Practitioners usually describe six steps, though two of them are rarely written down. The first is to define the decision: what action will differ depending on the result. For Gulal the action was binary, commit or do not, with a threshold of 35 per cent. The second step, the implicit one, is to write the threshold before fielding, because a number seen first invites a justification chosen afterwards.

The third step is sampling: choosing who receives the survey. The fourth is question writing, where the main rules are to ask about behaviour or choices rather than opinions on abstractions, to ask one thing per question, to offer balanced options including a fair way to say no, and to avoid loaded adjectives. The fifth is ordering and scaling: general questions before specific ones, because early items prime later ones, and a consistent response scale, because respondents drift toward the midpoint or the first option under fatigue. The sixth, also usually implicit, is piloting and screening: testing the draft on a handful of people while watching where they hesitate, and removing respondents whose answers show they did not read, such as those who finish in a third of the median time or answer every grid item identically.

Figure 1 shows what happened to Gulal’s invitations once these steps, and the ordinary friction of real people, were applied.

The chain compounds rather than adds. Of 2,50,000 invitations, 40.0 per cent were opened (1,00,000); 60.0 per cent of those started (60,000); 75.0 per cent of starters finished (45,000); and screening removed one in five completes, leaving 36,000. The completion rate, completes divided by invitations, was 45,000 divided by 2,50,000, or 18.0 per cent. The usable rate was 14.4 per cent. The Lagos headline had quietly assumed that the 85.6 per cent who never produced a usable answer would have answered like the 14.4 per cent who did.

4. A worked example, with a second pass

Gunwant asked for two checks. The first was a split test: 4,000 of the usable respondents were randomly divided into two arms of 2,000. Arm A saw the original agreement question. Arm B saw a neutral choice: You need to waterproof your home. Which would you buy: the standard coat at the usual price, or the ten-year coat at 30 per cent more?

The gap is 33.0 percentage points, 71.0 minus 38.0. Random assignment means the two arms are alike in who they are, so the whole gap belongs to the question. Agreement questions invite acquiescence, the tendency to say yes to a statement, and the phrase “protects your home for ten years” was an advertisement placed inside the question. Even the neutral 38.0 per cent sat only just above the 35 per cent bar.

The margin of error at 95 per cent confidence for a proportion is 1.96 times the square root of p(1 − p)/n, where p is the share and n the number of respondents. For p = 0.5 and n = 36,000 this is about 0.5 percentage points. For a subgroup of 400 it is about 4.9 points. But that margin captures only random sampling error, not the bias of who responded, which is the second check.

But metro customers are 30.0 per cent of Gulal’s buyers and 68.0 per cent of its respondents, because the app skews urban. Weighting re-counts each segment at its true share: 0.30 × 45.0 + 0.45 × 30.0 + 0.25 × 18.0 = 13.5 + 13.5 + 4.5 = 31.5 per cent. The decision flips. The threshold was 35 per cent; the weighted estimate is 3.5 points below it, and the answer changed because one input, the segment mix, changed. Notice that no amount of extra sample would have fixed this: more metro respondents only tighten the wrong estimate.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Leading is about effect, not intent

Nobody at Gulal meant to mislead. A question leads whenever its wording makes one answer easier than another. The test is empirical: split the sample and compare, as Table 1 did.

Sample size is not representativeness

36,000 sounds authoritative. The margin-of-error formula assumes a random draw from the population; an opt-in list from an app is not one. A large biased sample is a precise wrong answer.

Order effects are real and directional

If a survey asks about leaking walls and damp-related repair spending before the purchase question, respondents arrive primed to value waterproofing. Put the choice question first, or randomise block order so priming averages out.

Scale choices move the mean

A five-point agreement scale and a ten-point likelihood scale yield different averages for the same attitude. Habits such as favouring the positive end differ by language and region. Compare only like with like, and prefer reporting the share choosing a defined option over an average of vague numbers.

Stated intent overstates behaviour

Choosing the premium coat on a screen costs nothing. Real purchases face the dealer’s recommendation and the neighbour’s quote. Practitioners discount stated intent, and the honest reading of Gulal’s 38.0 per cent is a ceiling, not a forecast.

Surveys measure what, not why

A survey can show that tier-3 customers choose premium at 18.0 per cent. Whether price, mistrust or unfamiliarity explains it belongs to interviews.

Non-response is the silent half

The 2,05,000 invitees who never completed are not random. Compare early with late responders, and respondents with known customer data, to see which way the missing lean.

6. How it differs by context

In consumer products, the main risk is a self-selected, urban, app-active sample, as at Gulal; the remedy is quota or weighted design against known base shares. In B2B products, populations are small, perhaps a few hundred buyers, so the margin-of-error arithmetic is brutal: with 120 respondents, the margin at p = 0.5 is 1.96 × √(0.25/120) = about 8.9 points. B2B surveys therefore lean on targeted, named respondents and on respondent role, since the user, the approver and the payer often disagree. In marketplaces, there are two populations, such as dealers and homeowners, whose answers must be analysed separately because each side’s answer depends on its belief about the other.

An early-stage team usually has no panel; it surveys its own users, accepts the bias, and states it. A large company can buy panels and run randomised wording tests routinely, but faces institutional pressure: a number everyone hoped for rarely meets a sceptical reader.

7. Common mistakes

The persuasive question. Symptom: an unusually high agreement figure, quoted by the team that wrote the question. Misunderstanding: that wording is neutral packaging. Cheapest diagnostic: re-field the question as a choice between two neutral options to a random half of the sample.

Counting responses as the population. Symptom: a headline with no mention of who was invited and who answered. Misunderstanding: that a big n repairs bias. Diagnostic: tabulate respondents against known customer shares, as in Table 2.

The double-barrelled item. Symptom: respondents who disagree with themselves across items, such as “is the coat durable and affordable?” Misunderstanding: that related ideas make one question. Diagnostic: read each item aloud, listening for “and”.

Fielding before piloting. Symptom: many respondents leaving at one question. Misunderstanding: that a draft clear to its author is clear to others. Diagnostic: ten cognitive interviews, asking each person to restate what each question asks.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Gulal’s survey would have started with a one-line decision memo and the 35 per cent threshold, signed by Girdhari before fielding. The neutral choice question would have opened the survey. Invitations would have gone to a sample stratified across metro, tier-2 and tier-3 customers, using dealer-assisted channels for the last group, with quotas set at 30.0, 45.0 and 25.0 per cent. The funnel in Figure 1 would sit in the first slide, alongside the weighted estimate and a statement of what was not measured. The headline would state a weighted estimate and its limits, not a single number carrying more confidence than it has earned.

9. Closing

Gunwant took the weighted 31.5 per cent to Girdhari and the board. He did not recommend abandoning the product. He recommended a staged commitment: stock the premium coat only in metro and the larger tier-2 dealers, where segment results were 45.0 and 30.0 per cent, and run a dealer-assisted survey in tier-3 districts before extending. His reasoning: the survey had shown the headline was inflated but not whether a smaller launch cleared the bar, and sales data would settle that better than any survey.

To go further, study sampling and representativeness next, since Table 2 showed it can decide the outcome, and then conjoint and MaxDiff, which replace direct opinion questions with forced trade-offs and are less prone to the acquiescence in Table 1.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Gulal had fielded only the neutral question and received 38.0 per cent, which further checks would you still want before believing it, and in what order would you run them? Second, think of a survey result you have repeated in a meeting: which of the three conditions in Gunwant’s sentence could you actually demonstrate?

All figures are illustrative. Company and people are fictional; Asian Paints and Berger are named only as market context.
