Navpath Mobility: The Seventy-Five Per Cent Question

A teaching case on survey design

1. Opening

At twenty past nine on Monday, 19 October 2026, Ishwari Bapat sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the second floor of Navpath Mobility's office in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, with a slide that she had been told would be the most important one in the board deck. It carried a single number in forty-point type: 75% of delivery riders would switch to a Navpath electric scooter. The number came from a survey that had gone out to Navpath's rider waitlist three weeks earlier.

Bapat was Navpath's Head of Product. By Friday, 23 October, she had to recommend how many scooters the company should order from its assembly partner in Pune. The partner's price of ₹1.10 lakh per vehicle was held only until close of business that day, after which the partner's next open production slot was in January, and the vehicles had to be on the road before the Diwali fortnight, when food and grocery deliveries peak. The board would meet a week later, on 30 October, and would expect the order to have been placed on a clear rationale. The rationale, so far, was the slide. She had read the survey question that produced it twice that morning, and she was no longer sure it deserved forty-point type.

2. Company background

Navpath was founded in 2021 by two former automotive engineers who had watched delivery riders for Zomato, Swiggy and Zepto burn through petrol, and through a good part of their earnings, on dense city routes. The company bought electric scooters, bundled them with battery-swap access and servicing, and rented them to riders for ₹4,999 a month. By October 2026 it had about 1,150 vehicles on the road in Bengaluru. If every one were rented for all twelve months, that would come to annualised rental revenue of ₹6.90 crore (1,150 × ₹4,999 × 12).

The market around it was crowded and well funded. Yulu, Bounce and Zypp Electric all courted the same riders, Ather and Ola Electric sold directly to individual buyers, and petrol-bike rental shops in every neighbourhood undercut everyone on upfront cost. Subsidy under the central government's PM E-DRIVE scheme helped vehicle economics but was due to taper. In the summer, Navpath's board had approved a first fleet tranche of ₹15.00 crore from its latest round, to be released against evidence of demand. The waitlist, a list of 8,000 riders who had registered interest on the app, was the largest piece of evidence the company had.

3. The situation

In late September Navpath's growth team sent a survey, built in a hurry, to the waitlist. Of the 8,000 registrants, 6,400 carried a recorded consent that satisfied the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; the remaining 1,600 could not be contacted. The 6,400 invitations went out by WhatsApp and email, with a ₹50 UPI voucher for completion. Exhibit 1 sets out what happened.

The survey opened with an introductory screen that described Navpath as "India's most affordable, eco-friendly electric rental". Question 3 asked whether the respondent currently owned a petrol two-wheeler, and respondents who answered no were routed past the next block. Questions 5 and 6 asked how much rising petrol prices had hurt the respondent's earnings. Question 7 followed: "Would you switch to Navpath's affordable, eco-friendly electric scooter that saves you fuel costs and is easy to charge?" It was answered on a five-point scale from "Definitely would" to "Definitely not".

The 75.0 per cent on the slide is thus 840 of the 1,120 riders who were asked, and it is the most flattering of the rates in Exhibit 1, though the 83.3% completion rate is also respectable. Only a quarter of those invited finished the survey, and the 480 completers outside the petrol-owning group were never asked Q7 at all. Bapat could say with confidence only that 840 riders had ticked a favourable box.

Other evidence existed, and it did not agree. Between 14 September and 11 October, Navpath ran a soft pilot in Koramangala and HSR Layout. It offered the ₹4,999 monthly rental to 300 petrol-owning riders from registrants who did not start survey v1, so the pilot and the survey cover different riders, with a refundable deposit of ₹3,000. By the end of four weeks, 51 had signed, which is 17.0 per cent of the 300 offered.

The global team saw the survey differently from where they sat. In Berlin, the product designer had reviewed the draft at the end of his day and written a comment on Q7. In Toronto, the data scientist had been asked only to clean the export. In Singapore, the customer-success lead was hearing a version of the story from riders that the survey never captured. They liked the idea of an electric scooter, they said, but they dreaded the deposit and the queue at a swap station on a Friday night.

4. The people

Ishwari Bapat, Head of Product, Bengaluru, owns the recommendation. She joined Navpath from a payments company and has run concept tests but has never sized a hardware order. She wants a number she can defend to the board without hiding its weaknesses.

Ikram Bahl, Vice President of Partnerships, Jersey City, is a former sales head who has just closed a conversation with a large logistics client in Dubai, whose fleet team is waiting to hear how many Indian vehicles Navpath can guarantee. He wants the 3,000-vehicle order, because a bold fleet commitment wins partners and impresses investors, and he regards the survey as proof that demand is not the constraint.

Indrakshi Banthia, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai, controls the release of the ₹15.00 crore tranche. She has no quarrel with the product. Her concern is that a vehicle ordered and not rented earns nothing and loses value, and she distrusts any figure that arrives without its denominator.

Ingmar Berglund, Product Designer, Berlin, is the one who flagged Q7 in review, noting that it asked two things at once, price and charging, and praised the product while asking about it. The comment was left open overnight in Berlin's time zone, and the survey went out the next morning with the question unchanged. He wants it to be run again properly.

Ivy Boey, Customer Success Lead, Singapore, speaks to riders daily. She wants the deposit and swap-queue problems taken seriously before more vehicles are added to a fleet that is not yet delighting its current users.

5. The second test

Two weeks ago, after Berglund's objection, the Toronto data scientist ran a split-ballot test. Four hundred petrol-owning riders, each of whom had passed the same Q3 screen, were randomly assigned to two versions of the item. Version A used the original Q7 wording. Version B read: "Navpath rents an electric scooter for ₹4,999 a month, including battery swaps. Compared with what you spend now on your petrol vehicle, how likely are you to switch within the next three months?" Exhibit 2 shows the results.

The original wording reproduced the headline: 150 of 200, or 75.0 per cent. The neutral wording, which named the price, dropped the adjectives and asked about a time-bound switch, produced 86 of 200, or 43.0 per cent. The gap of 32.0 points is far outside sampling noise at 200 per arm. Because riders were randomly assigned, the difference is attributable to the wording package, which changed several things together: it named the price, dropped the adjectives, added a comparison with current spend and set a three-month window. The test cannot say which change did the work. Bapat noted that Version B was still a stated intention and still came from a self-selected waitlist.

Exhibit 3 translates the three candidate rates into vehicles. Survey v1 found that 70.0 per cent of completers owned a petrol vehicle. The 1,600 registrants without valid consent cannot be contacted, so Bapat applied that share only to the 6,400 consenting registrants, estimating 4,480 petrol-owning riders. She applied each rate to that figure, rounded to whole riders, and priced one vehicle per rider at ₹1.10 lakh.

6. The options

Option A: order 3,000 vehicles now. This follows the survey, with Ikram Bahl's reasoning behind it. At ₹1.10 lakh each the order costs ₹33.00 crore, which is ₹18.00 crore beyond the tranche and would need a bridge facility. It locks the price and the Pune production slot, it gives the Dubai conversation a number, and even the neutral-wording rate in Exhibit 3 fills only 1,926 of the 3,000 vehicles, leaving 1,074 idle. If riders behave as the pilot did (762), 2,238 vehicles sit idle, which is ₹24.62 crore of stranded capital.

Option B: pause and re-run the survey properly. A rewritten instrument, with single-barrelled items, neutral framing, the price stated and a sample drawn beyond the waitlist, would cost about ₹6.5 lakh and take three weeks, which would mean results around 9 November. The price hold would lapse, delivery would slip to January, and Navpath would miss the Diwali fortnight while Yulu, Bounce and Zypp Electric did not. The company would, however, buy nothing it could not defend.

Option C: order 1,350 vehicles within the tranche and fix the evidence in parallel. At ₹1.10 lakh this is ₹14.85 crore, inside the board's ceiling. In the meantime Navpath would field the corrected survey, take refundable ₹500 pre-bookings from the waitlist to observe behaviour rather than opinion, and have Boey's team test the deposit and swap-queue issues. The second lot would be sized on 20 November. The cost is exposure on the second lot, whose price may rise to about ₹1.15 lakh, which is 4.5 per cent more per vehicle, and a smaller story for Dubai.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Q7 aloud. What two things does it ask at once, and which words push the respondent toward yes? Why does that matter for how the 840 ticks should be read?
  2. In Exhibit 1, name the base for each rate. What fraction of everyone invited gave a positive answer, and what does the spread between 13.1 and 75.0 per cent tell you about the headline?
  3. Exhibit 2 shows a 32.0-point gap between two wordings. What does it tell you about the survey, and what does it not tell you about how many riders will rent? How do you reconcile the 43.0 per cent with the pilot's 17.0 per cent?
  4. Given the dates in Figure 1 and the ceilings in Exhibit 3, which of the three options would you take to the board, and what would you tell Ikram Bahl and Indrakshi Banthia?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. The central question in survey design is whether the answers can be believed. Q7 failed that test in three ways. It was double-barrelled, joining price and charging convenience, so a rider who found the scooter cheap but worried about charging had no honest answer. It was leading, because "affordable" and "eco-friendly" are praise. And it sat after two questions about the pain of petrol prices, which primed the very answer it wanted. The base mattered as well, because one number was quoted over the riders who were asked, while the funnel that produced them was far narrower. Exhibit 2 shows that a rewritten wording package moved the top-two box by 32.0 points.

What a good answer looks like. It does not throw away the survey. A good answer treats 43.0 per cent as a better but still optimistic upper estimate, because stated intent usually runs ahead of paid behaviour, and the pilot's 17.0 per cent included a ₹3,000 deposit that the survey never mentioned. It also notes that the sizing in Exhibit 3 leans on a waitlist of self-selected, consenting riders, so it cannot be generalised to Bengaluru. The bracket of 762 to 1,926 riders is wide, and a sound decision is sized to the low end while the evidence narrows.

One defensible path. Option C. A 1,350-vehicle order sits within the ₹15.00 crore tranche, preserves the Pune slot and covers the pilot-based demand of 762 with a margin of 588 vehicles. It stays inside Banthia's discipline: at the pilot rate 588 vehicles would sit idle, rather than 2,238 under Option A, and at the neutral-wording rate the lot would be fully used. The board slide should be replaced with a range and its bases, and Bahl can still tell Dubai that Navpath will commit to a second lot once the pre-bookings read out. The rewritten survey should split the double-barrelled item, state the price, randomise order, and report every rate over the riders actually shown each question.

Survey design: the instrument as a source of error

1. Two decisions, one instrument

At 7.40 on 9 October 2026, in a converted mill building in Pune, Yashodhan Mirajkar was arguing with his own pilot data. Mirajkar runs product for Yugantar Appliance Works, a maker of water purifiers that had spent two years putting a cellular module and a filter-life sensor into its mid-range line. The question before the board was a single number: how many units to build for the 2027 summer. A build of 28,000 units at a landed cost of ₹10,400 each commits ₹29.12 crore, mostly to components that cannot be cancelled after November. The survey meant to settle it had been fielded twice with identical question text and returned two answers — 62.0 per cent and 51.2 per cent said they would buy. Only the order of the five answer options had changed.

Eleven hundred kilometres away, in Gurugram, Zarna Ghatpande faced the mirror image. Ghatpande is head of customer experience at Zamaanat Credit Systems, which sells collections and underwriting software to non-banking financial companies and small finance banks regulated by the Reserve Bank of India. Its quarterly satisfaction tracker had risen for three consecutive quarters, from 41.2 per cent to 52.9 per cent on an unchanged question, and the chief executive had twice used that line to defer a ₹7.2 crore rebuild of the agent workflow. Reading the raw files, Ghatpande found that within every category of respondent the score had not moved at all.

The two cases are the same case: a number that looked like a measurement of the world was partly a measurement of the instrument. Survey design is therefore not a style guide for polite questions. It is error accounting — knowing which part of a figure came from respondents and which part the questionnaire manufactured, and refusing to spend money on the difference.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A survey is a standardised set of questions put to a sample so answers can be counted and projected onto a population. Survey design is the set of choices determining what those counts mean: the sample frame, the question stems, the response scale (the offered options and their labels), item order, the screening rules applied afterwards, and the definition of the reported statistic.

The field exists because the obvious model of a respondent is wrong. Rensis Likert's 1932 summated rating scale assumed a stable attitude waiting to be read off. By 1941 Donald Rugg had shown by split ballot that support for restricting speech moved more than twenty points depending on whether the question said "forbid" or "not allow", and Stanley Payne's The Art of Asking Questions (1951) catalogued dozens of such effects. The explanation came with the cognitive turn of the 1980s: Roger Tourangeau's four stages of comprehension, retrieval, judgement and response mapping; Norbert Schwarz on how context supplies the standard of comparison; and Jon Krosnick's 1991 account of satisficing. Don Dillman and Robert Groves then made the accounting explicit with total survey error: error has components — coverage, sampling, non-response, measurement, processing — they trade off, and a budget aimed at the wrong one is wasted.

Four schools disagree substantively. The psychometric school, descended from Likert, will sign that a multi-item scale with reported reliability measures a latent construct better than any single question; it will not sign that one behavioural choice item suffices. The total-survey-error school will sign that wording effects are usually smaller than non-response and coverage error and should be attacked second; it will not sign that a large opt-in panel becomes representative once weighted. The revealed-preference school, strongest in the Ehrenberg-Bass tradition and among experimentation teams, will sign that stated intent has no forecasting value; it will not sign that any attitude scale predicts purchase. The choice-modelling school, after Daniel McFadden, will sign that preference must be inferred from forced trade-offs, not that a direct top-two-box figure carries usable information. Mirajkar needs the third and fourth. Ghatpande needs the second.

3. Mechanics in depth

Yugantar's pilot, fielded to a purchased panel between 14 and 18 September 2026, tested one variable. Both arms saw an identical stem: If this purifier were available at ₹16,900, how likely is it that you would buy one in the next six months? Arm A saw the five options positive end first, Arm B negative end first; assignment was random, 2,500 completes per arm.

First, fix the reported statistic and its definition before fielding: top-two-box out of five is a decision rule, and a team that quietly becomes a top-three-box team has moved apparent demand by 18.0 points in Arm A without touching the product. Second, field the conservative arm — Yugantar's main wave, run to its app users between 5 and 9 October 2026, used negative-end-first ordering. Third, apply post-field screening with rules written in advance.

4. When the instrument can be trusted, and when it cannot

The conditions are statable as tests. First: can the respondent observe the thing asked about? Yugantar passes for price sensitivity and fails for filter-replacement behaviour, which buyers misremember; Zamaanat passes for workflow friction and fails for "would your institution renew", which agents do not decide. Second: is the sample frame the population the decision is about? Yugantar's main wave came from app users who already own a Yugantar product, while the build decision concerns new buyers — which is why that wave's 59.0 per cent sat above the purchased panel's 51.2 per cent at the same price. Zamaanat's frame is 1,180 named seats, which is the population, so coverage error is near zero and the problem is entirely who replies. Third: will the answer change the decision? If 28,000 units get built either way, the survey is theatre.

The idea is actively misleading in two situations. One is forecasting absolute demand from stated intent, quantified below at Yugantar's expense. The other is diagnosis: 57.0 per cent intent says nothing about why the other 43.0 per cent declined, and a team that reads the percentage as an explanation optimises the wrong variable.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product organisations fight over order. Yugantar sells purifiers, air coolers and water heaters; each line wants its block first, knowing the first block is unprimed. The honest resolution, randomised block order, costs power everywhere and is resisted by whichever line has the thinnest sample. Two-sided businesses face worse: a question about the other side measures belief, not fact, and Zamaanat's lender and agency distributions cannot be averaged.

Regulated settings constrain the instrument itself. Zamaanat cannot ask an agent about a named borrower's delinquency without creating a record it must then govern, and since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, consent for survey data must be specific and separable from product terms, so the response-boosting pre-tick is gone. Hardware-plus-software products need instruments a questionnaire cannot supply: Yugantar's evidence on taste and noise came from 180 placed units. AI-native products break self-report hardest, because users cannot tell a model's failure from their own prompt; workable instruments ask about the outcome ("did you send the draft unedited?") rather than the system.

At the organisational seam, research owns the instrument, marketing the panel budget, the product manager the decision, and nobody owns a tracker's comparability across years. Mature companies say they solve this with standards; what they do is keep a locked question bank with a change-control log, and batch wording improvements into a declared re-baselining every three or four years, because each one breaks the series.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Labels do more work than the number of points

A competent practitioner debates five points against seven. An expert knows the labels carry the meaning: "probably would buy" and "somewhat likely" are not the same option, and translating either into Hindi or Tamil shifts the distribution more than two extra points will. The tell: a tracker that jumped at the wave a translation vendor changed.

The midpoint is an exit, not a neutral position

Offering "might or might not" does not measure ambivalence; it offers a cheap escape from judgement, and removing it does not redistribute those people proportionally. In Arm A, 18.0 per cent took the midpoint. An expert reads a large midpoint as a sign the question was hard, and hunts the comprehension problem.

Acquiescence is cost minimisation, not politeness

The obvious reading is cultural deference; the better one is satisficing, since agreeing is cheaper than evaluating. The diagnostic is a reverse-keyed item: if "I would not consider changing my purifier" correlates positively with "I would consider changing my purifier", nobody is reading and the battery is suspect.

Order effects have a direction you can predict

Assimilation moves a later specific question toward the earlier general one; contrast moves it away. Asking about monsoon water quality before purchase intent primes the need and raises intent. Expert practice puts the decision question before anything that supplies a reason for it.

Top-two-box is a decision rule masquerading as data

The number of boxes is chosen, and at Yugantar the choice is worth 18.0 points. The tell is a deck where the box definition sits in a footnote, or changes between slides. An expert pre-registers it and reports the full distribution beside it, as Table 1 does.

Open-text answers are not a count of people

Themes are counted over those who wrote something, always a minority and the more opinionated one. Yugantar's largest theme was named by 523 people: 28.4 per cent of coded answers, but 8.2 per cent of usable respondents. Quoting the first to a pricing committee overstates the objection threefold.

Screening rules written after seeing the data are not rules

Because screening moved Yugantar's headline by 2.0 points, the rules are a lever. An expert fixes thresholds, attention-check wording and the disposition of failures before the field opens, and reports screened and unscreened figures both. The opposite announces itself as a methodology note whose speeder threshold is a round number arrived at late.

A tracker's real enemy is its own frame

Scores drift when the invitation list drifts, and lists drift silently because whoever maintains them is improving them. Ghatpande's case is the pure form. An expert publishes respondent composition beside the score and treats any wave whose mix moved beyond a declared tolerance as uninterpretable until decomposed. The obvious reading, that the product improved, is the one the data cannot support.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer physical goods, intent does not become purchase, so the survey's job is relative — which concept, which price step, which claim — and absolute levels need a calibration factor from history. In B2B and enterprise the constraint is population size and role. Zamaanat's 240 responses from 1,180 seats give a margin of error at a 50 per cent proportion of 1.96 times the square root of 0.25/240, or 6.33 points, narrowed to 5.65 by the finite-population correction, the square root of (1,180 − 240)/1,179, or 0.893. But the 240 came from only 138 accounts, 1.74 per account; at an intra-account correlation of 0.35 the design effect is 1 plus 0.74 times 0.35, or 1.26, so the effective sample is 240 divided by 1.26, or 191, giving 7.1 points. Clustering costs more than the finite population saves.

In platforms and marketplaces the two sides are reported separately, never blended. In hardware the survey screens before a home-use test rather than replacing it. In AI products novelty decays over weeks, so a single wave overstates satisfaction. By stage: a seed-stage team has no frame and should say so rather than weighting the bias away; a firm of Yugantar's size can afford split ballots, its highest-return research spend; a firm of Zamaanat's size has enough process to run a tracker for years with nobody owning its comparability.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Zamaanat's tracker: an improvement made entirely of composition

Zamaanat's tracker asks one question on an unchanged five-point scale and reports top-two-box. Respondents fall into three roles; the installed base holds 1,180 named seats: 905 collections agents, 212 branch managers and 63 heads of credit.

8.3 The 2025 failure, and what recovery looked like

In March 2025 Yugantar fielded a single-arm survey on a non-connected model at ₹14,900 and reported 34.0 per cent purchase intent across a frame of 1,20,000 app-identified prospects, implying 40,800 units. Finance approved 24,000, which is 58.8 per cent of the implied figure and felt conservative; at a ₹9,200 landed cost that is ₹22.08 crore of inventory. By March 2026 that audience had bought 9,840 units, or 8.2 per cent of the 1,20,000, leaving 14,160 unsold, cleared at ₹6,000 against ₹9,200 — a write-down of ₹4.53 crore. Recovery was arithmetic, not apology. The realisation rate — actual purchases divided by survey-implied purchases — was 9,840 divided by 40,800, or 24.1 per cent. 9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The unreplicated headline. Early sign: a number quoted with no arm, base or date. Diagnostic: what was the second arm? Cost late: the 2025 write-down of ₹4.53 crore, which a ₹3 lakh split ballot would have prevented.

Frame drift in a tracker. Early sign: a stable response count while the score moves smoothly one way. Diagnostic: publish the respondent mix beside the score. Cost late: two deferrals of the ₹7.2 crore rebuild, and a year of agent attrition attributed to pay.

Post-hoc screening. Early sign: a methodology note written after the analysis. Diagnostic: compare it with the pre-field document. Cost late: the series restarts.

Open-text inflation. Early sign: a theme share quoted without its denominator. Diagnostic: divide by usable respondents, not writers. Cost late: a roadmap re-sequenced for an objection held by 8.2 per cent and believed held by 28.4 per cent.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether to offer a midpoint. The remove-it camp holds that "might or might not" is pure satisficing, that forcing a side discriminates better, and that removal moves the positive share less than two points while reducing non-differentiation. The keep-it camp holds that forced choice fabricates opinion and is less stable on retest. Keep-it would be wrong if removal reliably improved out-of-sample prediction of behaviour; remove-it would be wrong if forced answers proved arbitrary, which retest studies sometimes suggest.

Whether weighting repairs non-response. Groves's heirs hold that weighting on variables correlated with both response and outcome genuinely reduces bias; sceptics, after a decade of polling misses, hold that it launders an unrepresentative sample into a confident one, because what drives non-response is usually unobserved. Ghatpande's case supports the first: role is observed, the seat mix known exactly. Yugantar's does not.

Whether to delete attention-check failures. Deleting raised Yugantar's data quality and lowered its headline by 2.0 points. The opposing position, held seriously in the methodology literature, is that attention checks disproportionately fail less-educated and non-first-language respondents, making deletion a coverage decision dressed as a quality one. It would be wrong if failure rates proved uncorrelated with demographics; deletion would be wrong if screened and unscreened samples predicted behaviour alike.

Whether to ask direct intent questions at all. The choice-modelling school says no and offers conjoint. Pragmatists answer that conjoint costs four to six times as much, needs a competent vendor, still measures stated behaviour, and that a calibrated direct question as in section 8.3 is cheaper per unit of decision quality. It stays unresolved because the comparison needs a realisation factor each firm must estimate from its own history.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied survey design writes better questions. Someone who has internalised it changes the order of work: the decision and its threshold first, the reported statistic defined before the instrument exists, a second arm budgeted as routine rather than begged for. They show distributions rather than headlines, with the respondent mix on the same slide as the score, and they can name which error component dominates — coverage at Yugantar, non-response at Zamaanat. Most distinctively, they state what their instrument cannot answer before being asked, because what they protect is the credibility of the next survey.

12. The decisions

On 13 October 2026 Mirajkar took three numbers to the board: 57.0 per cent screened intent, a 24.1 per cent realisation factor from 2025, and a calibrated 27,500 units. He recommended a first build of 22,000 with a component option on a further 8,000 exercisable in January, paying more per unit on the second tranche rather than repeating a ₹4.53 crore write-down. His reasoning: the survey could rank price points and name objections but not forecast a level, and only a staged commitment could.

Ghatpande did not report a corrected score. She reported that the tracker had measured nothing since December 2025, published the seat-weighted 37.7 per cent for all four waves, fixed the invitation list to a stratified sample matching the 905/212/63 seat mix, and declared W4 the new baseline. She then recommended funding the ₹7.2 crore rebuild on the 28.0 per cent agent score, which had never improved and never been visible.

Discussion questions. First, the app-user wave gave 59.0 per cent unscreened at ₹16,900 while a purchased panel gave 51.2 per cent at the same price: which is closer to the truth about new buyers, and what would you field to find out? Second, Ghatpande's correction makes her own function look bad for three quarters; what governance would have surfaced the frame drift without relying on her candour? Third, the realisation factor is 24.1 per cent on one product in one year: on what basis would you apply it to a connected product at a higher price?

13. Going deeper

Sampling and representativeness — study next: Zamaanat's whole error was a frame problem. Conjoint and MaxDiff — trade-offs instead of direct intent, removing the acquiescence that inflated Arm A. Quantitative concept testing — the norms and calibration factors section 8.3 improvised. Discrete choice and demand modelling — the apparatus behind refusing to ask directly. Qualitative vs quantitative research and synthesising research — where the codebook behind Table 4's kappa of 0.79 comes from. NPS, CSAT and CES and the Sean Ellis PMF survey — standard instruments, each wholly dependent on frame discipline. Measuring willingness to switch — the hardest intent question. Briefing a market research agency — where arms and screening rules get specified or lost. Descriptive statistics for PMs — design effect and finite-population correction. Home-use tests and sensory research — what Yugantar needed for noise and taste.

All figures are illustrative. Yugantar Appliance Works, Zamaanat Credit Systems and the people named are fictional; the Reserve Bank of India and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 appear only as market context.

Thirty-eight Per Cent of Whom? Pardaaz Money and the Plus Subscription

A case for discussion. The case does not resolve; several of the exhibits disagree with one another.

1. The night before

At nine on the evening of Sunday, 25 October 2026, Jyotsna Chivukula sat on the floor of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with eleven printed pages in two rows: the deck she would present to the Pardaaz Money board at ten next morning, and everything that made her unwilling to present it.

The second slide carried one number in 96-point type: 38%, captioned “38% of respondents would subscribe to Pardaaz Plus at ₹149/month.” Jagriti Chitale, who ran growth from Mumbai, had built the FY27 plan on it and sent that plan to two investors. Jyotsna had approved the slide on 15 September, and had spent the forty days since learning what respondents had been made to carry.

The sequence was not in dispute. Pardaaz invited 1,20,000 users to a survey, and 14,400 of the 1,20,000 invited opened it (12.0 per cent). But the price question sat behind a screen asking whether the user had ever faced a delay in withdrawing money. Only the 7,560 who said yes saw it, and 6,750 of the 7,560 shown it answered (89.3 per cent). The 2,565 enthusiastic answers were 2,565 of the 6,750 who answered it (38.0 per cent); also 2,565 of the 14,400 who started (17.8 per cent). Each such sentence names its own base; Exhibit 2A lists them. The base everyone reached for instead — the 9,000 who got to the submit screen — does not work at all: it neither contains all who answered the question nor excludes those never shown it.

Worse, the 6,750 were not a random slice of anything: two questions earlier they had said the product had already failed them in the way the paid feature promised to fix. Jerome Cheriyan, the data scientist in Toronto, put it on 28 August: “We asked the wound whether it wanted the bandage.”

Whether that made the number wrong or merely narrow, she could not decide. If 38 per cent of delay-sufferers would pay, and 7,560 of the 12,600 who reached the screen (60.0 per cent) were sufferers, there was a business in it; if the survey had taught people the word delay and sold it back, there was nothing. Monday was thirteen hours away.

2. Pardaaz Money, 2019–2026

Pardaaz Money Technologies Private Limited was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Jatan Chorghade and two classmates from the College of Engineering, Pune, on an unfashionable thesis: that what most salaried Indians wanted was not a demat account but somewhere to keep next month's rent that paid more than a savings account and came back the same day. The app swept idle balance into liquid mutual-fund schemes, settled withdrawals over UPI, and earned a commission in basis points. By July 2026 it had 41,80,000 registered users and 9,60,000 monthly transacting users, with a long Tier-2 tail nobody had studied. Series C closed in January 2026 at ₹540 crore, and the plan filed with it committed Pardaaz to ₹36 crore of subscription revenue in FY27 — a line item for a product that did not yet exist.

Two earlier decisions shaped October 2026. In March 2025 Pardaaz dissolved its two-person research team, saving about ₹62 lakh a year, and signed a 24-month retainer with Pramiti Research in Gurugram: ₹2.40 crore, twelve waves at ₹20 lakh a wave, with questionnaire design, scripting and panel access assigned to Pramiti. Change requests inside a wave cost ₹4.50 lakh and six working days. Ten of the twelve waves had been consumed.

The second was quieter. In 2024 Jitesh Chandekar's team in Pune built the in-app survey module in a fortnight, on the way to something else. It supported one skip condition per block; anything more meant putting a filter question in front of a block and dropping everyone who answered the wrong way. Nobody recorded that as a research constraint — it was a ticket in a sprint. It is why the price question sat behind the delay screen: not a researcher's choice, but a module that could not route two conditions at once.

3. The industry

The Indian savings-and-investing app market in 2026 was crowded at the top and strange underneath. Groww and Zerodha's Coin held the direct-mutual-fund mindshare, Paytm Money and Navi competed for the first-time investor, Jio Financial Services outspent everyone, and every large bank had shipped a goal-based savings tab. Differentiation on returns was impossible: the schemes were the same schemes, so convenience was what remained — which is why four companies were converging on one promise, money out, instantly.

That promise was regulated. SEBI's instant access facility for liquid schemes is capped at ₹50,000 or 90 per cent of folio value per day, whichever is lower; above that, redemption follows the ordinary cycle. “Instant withdrawal” was therefore true for the median user and false for the user with ₹3 lakh parked before a property payment — precisely the user whose balance made the subscription worth selling. UPI limits added a second ceiling; the DPDP Act added a third, on research rather than product, since the March 2025 consent notice covered research through in-app channels and said nothing about telephone re-contact.

Pardaaz's exposure was not only domestic. Since 2024, non-resident Indians in the Gulf had been onboarded through Panchvati Global DMCC in Dubai, which held exclusive UAE distribution until March 2028 and contributed about ₹9.4 crore of annualised revenue — small, but the fastest-growing line. Javed Contractor, who ran Panchvati, had his own panel vendor and a contractual right to be consulted on co-branded pricing.

4. The situation in detail

In June 2026 Jinal Chokshi, who had joined in February as Pardaaz's first Head of Insights since the outsourcing, ran eighteen depth interviews in Pune, Coimbatore and Lucknow. 11 of the 18 interviews (61.1 per cent) described a problem that was not slowness but unpredictability: respondents could not tell, at the moment of pressing withdraw, whether money would arrive in four minutes or the next working day, and kept a float elsewhere. Four named the ₹50,000 cap. Not one used the word delay unprompted.

The instrument that went to Pramiti on 14 July translated unpredictability into delay, because delay was countable. Jonas Czarnecki, the designer in Berlin, suggested showing the benefit before the price; Pramiti's scripting lead, Jashodhara Chalapathi, proposed randomising the order instead — the only methodological improvement anyone made to Wave 10.

Wave 10 fielded from 11 to 18 August. The frame was the 11,40,000 users who had opened the app in the seven days to 10 August with push enabled; 1,20,000 of the 11,40,000 were invited (10.5 per cent). Exhibit 1 sets out each item's base. Pramiti's topline arrived on 21 August, the bases in an annexe nobody opened: 80 per cent agreement with the benefit statement, 38 per cent intent at ₹149. Jagriti's model went into the FY27 plan on 15 September, and the plan-review slide she built for it, now second in tomorrow's deck, said simply “38% of respondents”.

Three things then went wrong, each found by someone with an interest in its going wrong. On 28 August Jerome Cheriyan, reconciling the survey export against the event stream, found the skip — and, from the user IDs, that the paywall test and the survey had drawn on overlapping samples, so the two studies could no longer be called independent samples; Exhibit 5's footnote carries the counts.

On 2 September, nineteen days after the field midpoint, Pramiti re-asked the price question to 1,600 of those who had answered it, and 1,000 of the 1,600 re-invited replied (62.5 per cent). Exhibit 6B is the cross-tabulation: the same people, same wording, nineteen days apart, agreed with themselves on 570 of 1,000 occasions, a kappa of 0.35. Jinal circulated it with a line: “This is the number I would put on slide two.”

On 8 October Javed Contractor sent a study his own team had commissioned in Dubai: 640 completes, 70 per cent top-two intent at AED 9 a month on a seven-point scale. His note read: “Your 38 is conservative.” Exhibit 2B prints it, and why it cannot be set beside Exhibit 2A.

And on 20 October, counsel asked whether the 2 September re-contact was covered by the March 2025 DPDP notice. The question was not settled: if the answer was no, the kappa — the most damaging figure Pardaaz possessed — might not be citable in a filing, though nothing stopped Jyotsna citing it to her board.

5. The people

Jyotsna Chivukula, Senior Director of Product, Bengaluru. Owns Plus; approved the 38 per cent slide on 15 September, two weeks after the base problem surfaced. Wants the board to hear a range, but her FY27 objectives require a double-digit attach rate — which a range straddling 2 per cent is not. Unsaid: Jatan does not know about the kappa, and she suspects the construct was her own error.

Jatan Chorghade, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Holds that research sizes an opportunity rather than approving one; wants Plus live before the festive quarter closes, with two investors holding the plan and a Series D coming. Unsaid: he wrote the ₹36 crore into the Series C plan himself, against advice.

Jagriti Chitale, Vice-President, Growth, Mumbai. Argues the survey is the only forward-looking evidence and the paywall test a fortnight's artefact of a bad card; her variable pay tracks FY27 subscription revenue. Unsaid: Jerome copied her on the base problem on 10 September, and she put the caveat in the appendix.

Jinal Chokshi, Head of Insights, Bengaluru (joined February 2026). Wants a re-field on a clean base before anybody commits a number; a credible failure argues for rebuilding research in house. Unsaid: she converted “unpredictability” into “delay”, and the double-barrelled statement in Exhibit 2A is in her own hand on the 14 July draft.

Jerome Cheriyan, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Holds that only the 2.1 per cent is evidence; an experimentation platform he has proposed twice would be funded by a win for revealed preference. Unsaid: his test ran at one price, through a card his own team built in two days, and he published a conversion figure knowing 192 trials were unresolved.

Jonas Czarnecki, Principal Designer, Berlin. Holds that the survey measured the concept, not the price, and that Form B is the honest order because it is the order a user meets in the app. Unsaid: his brief described a feature SEBI's cap will not let Pardaaz deliver above ₹50,000 a day.

Reports that escalations cluster around timing promised and then missed, not slowness, and warns that a paid “instant” tier turns a complaint into a contractual grievance. Unsaid: her taxonomy folds “delay” and “unclear timing” into one code, so she cannot prove the distinction.

Wants a UAE launch on 1 November at a co-branded AED 9, on his own study; his revenue share pays on gross subscription value, not retention. Unsaid: his vendor sampled from his own customer list, and he has already told two relationship managers the launch is confirmed.

8. The options as Jyotsna sees them

One: present the 38 per cent with its base disclosed, and hold the 1 November launch at ₹149. It keeps the plan, Javed and the release train — and commits Pardaaz to a figure describing the willingness of self-identified sufferers to buy relief from suffering.

Two: present the post-stratified 33.2 per cent of Exhibit 4B and ask the board to re-cut FY27. This looks like rigour and is partly theatre: weighting repairs the language skew and leaves the screening skew in place. It would force a conversation about the ₹36 crore, which needs 2,01,300 of the 9,60,000 transacting users (21.0 per cent) to pay — ten times what the paywall test produced.

Three: spend one of the two remaining Pramiti waves on a corrected instrument. No delay screen in front of the price item, one randomised order, the double-barrelled statement broken into three, two more languages, and a question about predictability rather than delay. ₹20 lakh of retainer value, six working days for the change request, ten days in field — so no number before the board meeting, or before the 29 October cut-off.

Four: declare stated intent unusable and decide on revealed preference alone. Launch to a larger randomised slice at two or three price points and tell the board the attach rate will be known in six weeks. It costs five engineer-weeks, the ONDC connector slipping past the festive quarter, and a board asked to back a product whose revenue line is ₹1.50 lakh a month.

Under the four Jyotsna wrote a fifth line that was not an option but a worry. All four assumed the thing to measure was willingness to pay ₹149 for faster withdrawals; the eighteen interviews had not said that. And SEBI's ₹50,000 ceiling meant that for the largest balances — the ones whose subscription economics worked — “instant” was a promise Pardaaz could not keep at any price. If that was right, Exhibit 2A measured demand for a product that could not be built, and the right Monday answer was not a number at all.

The board meets at 10:00 IST on Monday, 26 October 2026. The release train for the festive build cuts off on 29 October; anything not merged ships after Diwali, into a quarter in which Pardaaz does a third of its annual new-user volume. Money constrains the research, not the launch. Two waves remain, worth ₹40 lakh of the ₹2.40 crore retainer; an instrument change inside a wave costs ₹4.50 lakh and six working days; an out-of-retainer wave is quoted at ₹26 lakh. At ₹20 lakh a wave, Wave 10's 6,750 price-item answers cost about ₹296 each. A telephone study of Tier-2 and Tier-3 users in their own languages is quoted at ₹34 lakh for 1,200 completes, about ₹2,833 a complete — nine and a half times the in-app figure, and the only route to the 3,45,600 transacting users Wave 10 excluded. A four-city in-person study of 60 respondents would cost ₹11 lakh, ₹18,333 a respondent.

People constrain it further. Jitesh's team is two engineers, committed to the ONDC connector; two skip conditions per block is a five-week change. Jinal is the entire Insights function. And a fresh offline sample needs a new DPDP notice and, counsel estimates, a fortnight of review, while the status of the 2 September re-contact — and therefore of the kappa — remains open.
